items.prompt: Now 12:00. First response was due 11:30 but was answered at 11:45; resolution is due 13:00; a 30-minute rule exists. Does the sweep escalate?
items.answer: No: once answered, only the future resolution clock counts
distractors: Yes: the first-response deadline was breached by 30 minutes before the answer
Yes: the earliest deadline is always active
No: the 30-minute rule needs strictly more than 30 breached minutes to fire
items.explanation: dueAt is resolutionDueAt when firstResponseAt is set; otherwise it is the earliest of both deadlines.

items.prompt: Unanswered ticket, first response due 11:30, now exactly 12:00, one rule with afterMins 30. What happens?
items.answer: It escalates: 30 breached minutes meets afterMins <= breachedMinutes
distractors: Nothing yet: the rule needs breachedMinutes strictly greater than 30
Nothing: overdueMinutes rounds 30 down to 29
It escalates twice, once for each breached clock on the ticket
items.explanation: Eligibility is inclusive; a test exactly at the threshold pins that boundary.

items.prompt: What does overdueMinutes return for a deadline 89 seconds ago, and for one 10 minutes in the future?
items.answer: 1 and 0: it floors complete minutes and clamps future deadlines to zero
distractors: 2 and -10: it rounds to the nearest minute and keeps the sign of the difference
1 and -10: negative values mark tickets that are not yet due

items.prompt: Why does rule selection break ties on id after sorting by afterMins descending?
items.answer: So equal thresholds route the same way on every run
distractors: Because ids encode creation time and older rules take priority by business policy
localeCompare is faster
To pick the smallest eligible threshold first when several rules apply to one ticket
items.explanation: Without the id tie-break, rules with equal afterMins would be ordered however the database returned them, so identical data could route to different groups on different runs. A deterministic order makes the sweep and its tests reproducible.

items.prompt: Two sweep workers try to escalate the same ticket at once. What guarantees only one succeeds?
items.answer: The conditional update WHERE escalatedAt IS NULL
distractors: A unique index on the escalatedAt column
An in-process mutex per ticket held by the sweep while it decides and writes
Prisma's updateMany serializes concurrent calls that target the same id
items.explanation: Compare-and-set: 'change this row only if the world still looks the way I thought it did'.

items.prompt: Two staff members post public replies at nearly the same instant. Whose timestamp becomes firstResponseAt?
items.answer: The first to commit; the second matches zero rows
distractors: The later one, since the last write always wins on an update
The earlier client timestamp, compared inside the update statement itself
Both
items.explanation: markFirstResponse uses where { id, firstResponseAt: null }, so the first writer wins.

items.prompt: An assignment request body is { reason: "keep" } with no assigneeId. What happens to the ticket's assignee column?
items.answer: Untouched: undefined leaves the column alone
distractors: It is cleared, because a missing assigneeId is coerced to null before the update
Set to the requester
The request is rejected because assigneeId is a required field on every assignment
items.explanation: { assigneeId: null, reason: 'clear' } clears it; omission preserves it.

items.prompt: An admin moves a ticket to group g2 with { supportGroupId: "g2" }; its assignee belongs to g1. What does the service send to the repository?
items.answer: The group move plus assigneeId: null
distractors: Only the group move; the g1 assignee stays attached to the ticket
A 409, because group moves require an explicit new assignee in the same request
The move, with the assignee transferred to g2
items.explanation: Otherwise no group-scoped list query would return the ticket for its assignee: an invisible routing state.

items.prompt: An assignment's conditional write matches zero rows because the ticket changed after it was read. What does the caller get, and is an audit row written?
items.answer: A ValidationDomainError asking to retry, and no assignment audit
distractors: Success with the stale data, plus an audit row noting the conflict
A database exception surfaced as a 500, plus an audit row
A silent no-op 200
items.explanation: assign returns null when count is 0; the service turns that into a domain error before the audit write. The loser learns it lost from the row count, not from an exception.

items.prompt: Why is roleCapabilities[user.role]?.includes(capability) ?? false wrong for a session whose role is "constructor"?
items.answer: The lookup finds the inherited Object constructor, so .includes throws and a 403 becomes a 500
distractors: It returns true, granting every capability to the 'constructor' role
Nothing: optional chaining treats inherited properties as undefined
TypeScript rejects 'constructor' as a role at runtime
items.explanation: hasOwnProperty.call plus Array.isArray makes the helper fail closed (false) for inherited keys like constructor, toString and __proto__.

items.prompt: An escalation target group is invalid in one case; in another, a concurrent worker already escalated the ticket. How do the two negative paths differ?
items.answer: The invalid target never reaches markEscalated; the race loser does and gets null
distractors: Both call markEscalated, which throws for each of them
The invalid target is audited as rejected; the race loser throws a 500
They are indistinguishable
items.explanation: Test both: refactors often start auditing rejected targets or turn normal races into noisy errors.

items.prompt: A test sets claimed = true in a fake and calls it twice, observing one escalation. What does that prove?
items.answer: Only the service's control flow against a fake
distractors: That the conditional update is race-safe against a real PostgreSQL instance
That the ticket and its audit row are written in one database transaction
Nothing; delete the test
items.explanation: A stronger fake models conditional update counts and rollback snapshots; state the remaining limitation whenever quoting the test.

items.front: The three compare-and-set predicates in ticketRepository, read as sentences
items.back: Escalate only if escalatedAt is null (and status is what the sweep saw); set firstResponseAt only if it is still null; assign only if firstResponseAt, status and group still match what the caller read. 'Change this row only if the world still looks the way I thought it did.'

items.front: Why do SLA and assignment invariants live in services and repositories, not the dashboard form?
items.back: Every route, job and future worker must share them; a UI check protects only one entry point. They are domain invariants, not UI preferences.

items.front: Five observable properties of a strong escalation solution
items.back: Selects the earliest still-active deadline; ignores first-response deadlines once answered; picks only a rule whose threshold is reached; validates the target user/group before any write; includes escalatedAt: null and the expected status in the claim, with ticket + audit written in one transaction by the real adapter.

items.front: Why can a ticket escalate only once, and what would multi-tier escalation need?
items.back: The schema has only escalatedAt, used as a durable one-escalation claim. Multi-tier escalation would need rule identity on the claim or a separate escalation event table.
